parsed_answer.content: WebFlux and Virtual Threads represent two distinct architectural paradigms for achieving high-concurrency in the JVM ecosystem. WebFlux is built upon the Reactive Streams specification and Project Reactor, utilizing an event-loop model (Netty) where a small, fixed number of threads handle non-blocking I/O operations. It relies on functional programming primitives like Mono and Flux to orchestrate asynchronous pipelines, effectively decoupling the request-handling thread from the I/O wait time. Conversely, Virtual Threads, introduced in Project Loom (JDK 21+), shift the concurrency burden from the application code to the JVM runtime. Instead of forcing developers to write non-blocking, asynchronous code, Virtual Threads allow for a traditional imperative, blocking programming style while maintaining massive scalability. The JVM multiplexes these lightweight, stack-copying threads onto a small pool of carrier platform threads, allowing a single application to hold millions of concurrent connections without the overhead of context switching inherent in OS-level threads.

items: WebFlux achieves efficiency by never blocking the carrier thread; if a database call is made, the thread is released back to the pool, and a callback resumes the execution later.

Virtual Threads achieve efficiency by 'parking' the virtual thread when a blocking operation (like socket read) occurs, unmounting it from the carrier thread so the carrier can execute other virtual threads.

In WebFlux, thread-local variables are dangerous and often unsupported due to the asynchronous nature of execution; Virtual Threads support ThreadLocals, though they should be used with extreme caution to avoid memory bloat.
Virtual Threads eliminate the 'colored function' problem where you must maintain separate sync and async APIs throughout your codebase.

parsed_answer.content: A critical production gotcha: Virtual Threads are not a 'magic bullet' for CPU-bound tasks. If you perform heavy computation (e.g., image processing, complex math) inside a Virtual Thread, you will pin the carrier thread, effectively negating the scalability benefits. Always use a dedicated ForkJoinPool or similar executor for CPU-intensive work, regardless of whether you are using WebFlux or Virtual Threads.
